fun_highlights: The callback system genuinely earns its payoffs in the transcript: 'cb_books_late' closing the loop on a childhood card held for 43 years (Calla Okonkwo, age 50, 'Read, at last with ease, the book that began everything at age 7'), the 'cb_lookaway' card delivering a decades-late reckoning in Mira Halloran and Emory Lindqvist. These are the moments that make a 3-minute session feel dense — you chose something at 7 and it lands at 49.

The era system provides real session-variety at zero player cost. In a single read: war (Elias Okonkwo drafted at 23, Caleb Castellane posting out before the wedding), plague (Hale Okonkwo keeping his distance at 23 and living with 'the arithmetic of it'), plenty (Cleo Castellane watching 'the fat years make fortunes and stayed, deliberately, modest'). Each era genuinely changes which cards fire and how the world-opening line reads.

The dynasty layer delivers visible payoff moments at short-session cadence: the motto crystallising ('The family's character has settled, at last, into words'), the house-seat rising mid-life ('The family climbed in the world this generation'), and the bequest framing at succession ('From Lucan, deliberately: nothing but your own freedom'). A mobile snacker gets a clear reward beat every few lives without needing to commit to a long arc.

Vocation-specific arcs (a_soldier_service, m_soldier_ghost, a_scholar_question, etc.) genuinely differentiate lives structurally. The 15 transcripts show soldiers going to campaigns and haunted by them, scholars paying off their study and choosing to teach or guard the knowing, makers opening shops and facing the masterwork question, wanderers settling or not. The cards are not interchangeable texture — they create different narrative shapes.

The prose quality at its best is the strongest card in the deck for the genre. Lines like 'There is a whole life she keeps behind the eyes, and visits often' (Dynasty 1, obs), 'Married Annika long after the age for it, and was privately astonished to be so happy so late' (Dynasty 7), and 'Took the warning seriously — changed the work, the food, the hours — and bought herself years' (Dynasty 9) are the kind of writing that earns a 'one more life' impulse.

Trait affinity weighting in drawCard() is a real structural differentiation mechanism — bookish children genuinely lean toward c_book (2.6x weight), warm toward c_friend, restless toward c_steal and c_move. Looking at the transcripts, a 'bookish' Tobias Aldecott keeps the book at 11; a 'guarded' Beatrix Okonkwo hides her gift at 9. The childhood pattern genuinely differs.
staleness: The 'meet them halfway' / 'pretend not to notice' love-opening plays in almost every life that gets love, and the phrasing of the followed choice is templated enough to register. Across 15 dynasties I counted: 'Started spending time with someone...', 'Fell in love — the kind that quietly rearranges the furniture of a life', 'Fell in love, and was surprised, as everyone is, that it was her this time', 'Fell in love, and was aware, with a cold clarity...', 'Found, without looking, the person the rest of the life would arrange itself around', 'Fell, with no particular grace...', 'Let someone in, the whole way, for the first time', 'Started, without quite deciding to, building the days around another person' — these are all from y_love1/a_meet_late's freshPick pool and they share the same emotional beat. Seven out of eight are some variant of 'fell, surprised, rearranged.' A mobile snacker across multiple short sessions will pattern-match fast.

The 'Be known as learned / hard to cross / open-handed' reputation card (a_make_name) fires in a high fraction of adult lives and the logLine phrasing is nearly identical every time: 'Set out, deliberately, to be the one the family came to for answers' / 'Set out, deliberately, to be the one no one tried twice' / 'Set out, deliberately, to be the one the door was always open at.' The 'Set out, deliberately, to be the one [X]' template is audible across Dynasty 2 (age 38), Dynasty 4-Noor (age 32), Dynasty 4-Hale (nothing), Dynasty 5 (nothing), Dynasty 6-Tomas (nothing), Dynasties 7, 10, 11, 13-Greta, 14-Greta. When it fires, the framing is always the same sentence skeleton.

The body-decline ambient observations (vit_tire pool) appear in nearly every post-45 life and share a very similar grammar across their large pool: '[They] has started to plan the day around what the body will permit', 'The weather has begun living in their joints, and forecasting badly', 'Their legs know something the rest of them is not yet ready to hear', 'The body has begun sending its small bills, and expecting them paid'. The engine's per-life cap of 4 obs helps but doesn't eliminate the pattern — in a long life (Henrik at 85, Selma at 82) 3–4 of these appear and the register is samey. A 3-minute snacker who plays back-to-back sessions will feel the body-decline section as an expected speed bump.

The marriage logLine pool's 'late marriage' sub-pool is deployed correctly (age > 48 gate) but over-fires in the transcripts because the engine's moderate nudge still clusters a lot of marriages in the 40s–50s. Result: 'Married [X] late, and found the lateness made the vow weigh more', 'Married [X] after both had long stopped expecting it, and meant it the more for that', 'Married [X] long after the age for it, and was privately astonished to be so happy so late', 'Married [X] when both had given up the expecting' appear in Dynasties 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15. The trope of 'late love, all the sweeter' is the dominant marriage register in this corpus. The young-marriage variants are underrepresented.

The 'drifter arc' identity at midlife — the 'Ache, quietly, for an anchor' vs 'Lean into the range. Be unplaceable' beat — repeats verbatim across multiple drifter lives and the logLines are identical: 'Felt, under the freedom, the particular tiredness of the unanchored — the envy, now and then, of people who knew what they were' (Vesna Thorne) vs the same framing in Noor Okonkwo, Anders Aldecott, Mira Halloran. For a genre that lives or dies on each life feeling singular, four lives sharing an identical self-reckoning sentence is the clearest staleness failure in the corpus.

The 'a_belief' card (faith question) fires in a high fraction of lives and its two outcomes — 'Made a quiet peace with something larger than herself, and carried it lightly' and 'Left the largest question open, and found she could live there comfortably enough' — both read as quiet closure. Neither option carries much narrative weight, and both logLines have an identical tonality of 'nothing was decided.' Across Saoirse (D1), Henrik (never fires but close), Calla Okonkwo (left open), Ottilie Ashby (left open), Selma Quint (left open), Mira Halloran (never), Greta Aldecott (made peace), Saoirse Brandt (left open): the card is frequent and its outcomes are near-indistinguishable in tone.

improvements.what: Add a second structural logLine variant for love-opening outcomes that uses a DIFFERENT metaphor than 'rearranged / fell / surprised'. Specifically: the y_love1 'Meet them halfway' pool currently has 8 variants but 7 share the fall/surprise/rearranged register. Add 4–6 lines that approach love from the opposite direction — the person who CHOSE it deliberately, who is not surprised, who notices it like a business decision and is undone anyway. This creates range within the pool.
improvements.why: The love-opening is the single highest-traffic narrative beat in the transcripts (every partnered life hits it). Its sameness is the first pattern a returning mobile snacker will notice. Widening the register costs nothing and has immediate session-feel impact.

improvements.what: Add a 'late-verse' variant to the a_make_name card's logLines that does NOT use the 'Set out, deliberately, to be the one [X]' skeleton. The card fires in most adult lives and the current three-line pool has the same opening clause across all three outcomes. Even one additional outcome per branch that approaches the reputation-setting from a different angle (e.g. a character realising it has already happened, rather than choosing it) would reduce the template-feeling.
improvements.why: The a_make_name card appears in roughly half the adult lives in the corpus. Its current logLine construction is audibly identical every time it fires. For a mobile snacker it reads as 'the reputation card' rather than a moment.

improvements.what: Gate the drifter-arc midlife self-reckoning card (m_adrift_reckon) more tightly on memory flags so that it does NOT produce identical logLines across lives. Specifically: the two drifter outcomes ('Ache, quietly, for an anchor' and 'Lean into the range') should have their logLines vary by WHAT the character has actually done — a drifter who has a child should reckon with it differently than one who doesn't; one who 'let_home' should have a different texture than one who 'stayed_home'. The identical 'particular tiredness of the unanchored' sentence in Vesna Thorne and the same beat in Noor, Anders, Mira is the most literal repetition in the transcripts.
improvements.why: The drifter arc is the only vocation that can repeat exact logLine text across multiple lives in a single read because its pool isn't memory-parameterized like the callbacks are. This is the easiest cross-life staleness to fix.

improvements.what: Reduce the frequency of the vit_tire ambient observation cluster in long lives, or add a sub-pool that fires only once per 15 years of age and draws from a NON-body register (mood, memory, relationship texture) as an alternative aging-observation. The current vit_tire pool is large (18 lines) but shares the body-clock grammar across all of them. A life from 50–89 currently generates 2–4 near-identical body-decline ambient lines as a predictable 'settling into old age' texture block.
improvements.why: For a mobile snacker playing a long life in multiple sessions, the body-decline texture is the most predictable stretch. It reads as a mandatory slow zone rather than characterful aging.

improvements.what: Introduce 2–3 additional callback cards that fire on COMBINATIONS of memories not currently exploited: a soldier who also 'looked_away' (bearing witness vs bearing arms), a maker who 'stayed_straight' for a long life (craft and integrity compounding), a scholar who had 'early_restless' (intellectual restlessness vs scholarly settlement). The current callback system is strong but most callbacks are 1-memory-to-1-callback. Cross-memory callbacks would make lives with rare combinations feel singular in a way the current system does not.
improvements.why: The best moments in the transcripts are the multi-layered callbacks — the book read at 7 returned at 50 WITH the affair confession still pending. More combinations of this type would reward varied play and differentiate the 4th and 5th runs without requiring new card volume.

verdict: A Life is genuinely better than most games in this genre at avoiding staleness within a single dynasty — the callback arc, vocation differentiation, and era system all do real work, and the prose quality at its peak is good enough to earn the 'one more life' pull. But across multiple short sessions, the mobile snacker will hit a recognizable template: love opens with a fall/rearrange metaphor, the adult years include the reputation card and the belief card in near-identical phrasing, the drifter arc produces literally repeated sentences across lives, and the body-decline stretch is a predictable slow zone. The score reflects a game that has solved the hardest structural problems (dynasty layer, callback reach-backs, vocation arcs) but has left high-traffic surface-level prose less varied than those structural wins deserve.
